title: The Concepts Database — Overview: what a concept record teaches
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. A concept is a reusable unit of understanding — learn feedback loops once and you recognize them in thermostats, markets, and ecosystems. Each record in this database teaches one concept five ways: a plain definition, a concrete example, a memorable analogy, real applications across fields, and a working demonstration you can run. Concepts are ladder-ranked from simple to complex so a learner can climb. Knowing the name of a concept is the beginning; this database aims at the working understanding that lets you use it.
capabilities: Five-way teaching: definition, example, analogy, application, demonstration
Reusable understanding across fields
Ladder-ranked from simple to complex
Working understanding as the goal, not vocabulary

title: The Concepts Database — Feedback loops
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. A feedback loop feeds a system's output back into its input. Negative feedback opposes change and creates stability — a thermostat cuts heat when the room warms, cruise control eases off uphill speed. Positive feedback amplifies change and creates runaway — a microphone near its speaker squeals louder and louder, panic selling drives prices down which drives more selling. Engineers design with negative feedback for control and watch for positive feedback as a failure mode. The demo iterates both kinds so you can feel the difference: one settles, one explodes.
capabilities: Negative feedback: opposes change, creates stability
Positive feedback: amplifies change, creates runaway
Thermostats and cruise control as designed examples
Positive feedback as an engineering failure mode

demo.title: Negative vs positive feedback iteration
demo.code: function neg(x){let v=x;for(let i=0;i<20;i++)v+=(10-v)*0.3;return +v.toFixed(2);}function pos(x){let v=x;for(let i=0;i<10;i++)v*=1.3;return +v.toFixed(0);}J({negative_to_10:neg(0),positive_from_1:pos(1)});assert(Math.abs(neg(0)-10)<0.05&&pos(1)>10,'feedback');

title: The Concepts Database — Entropy
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Entropy measures disorder — or equivalently, missing information. In thermodynamics it says isolated systems drift toward disorder: hot coffee cools, tidy rooms mess themselves. In information theory, Shannon entropy measures the average surprise per message: a fair coin carries one bit of entropy per flip; a double-headed coin carries zero because there is no surprise. Engineers fight entropy with maintenance, insulation, and error correction, and they measure it to know how much signal a channel can carry. The demo computes Shannon entropy for a biased coin.
capabilities: Thermodynamic entropy: systems drift toward disorder
Shannon entropy: average surprise per message
Fair coin one bit, fixed coin zero bits
Fighting entropy: maintenance, insulation, error correction

title: The Concepts Database — Abstraction
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Abstraction hides complexity behind a simpler interface: you drive a car with pedals and a wheel, not by timing fuel injectors. Good abstractions leak little — the interface tells the truth about what lies beneath — while bad ones force you to learn the hidden layer anyway. Layers of abstraction stack: applications sit on operating systems, which sit on hardware, each layer hiding the one below. The power is reuse — one well-built abstraction serves a thousand programs — and the price is opacity when it breaks. The demo builds a tiny abstraction layer over raw values.
capabilities: Hiding complexity behind simpler interfaces
Good abstractions leak little; bad ones force hidden learning
Layered stacks: apps on OS on hardware
Reuse as the power, opacity as the price

title: The Concepts Database — Calibration
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Calibration aligns an instrument with reality: compare its readings against a known standard, record the error, and correct future readings. A scale is calibrated with certified weights; a thermometer with ice water and boiling water; a sensor with a reference instrument. Calibration has an expiry — instruments drift — so schedules and certificates track when each device was last aligned and when it is due again. Uncalibrated measurement is guessing with digits. The demo applies a two-point calibration correction to raw readings.
capabilities: Comparing readings against known standards
Two-point calibration: ice water and boiling water
Drift and expiry: calibration schedules and certificates
Uncalibrated measurement is guessing with digits

title: The Concepts Database — Redundancy
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Redundancy keeps spares so failure does not mean catastrophe: two engines on an airliner, RAID mirrors for disks, backup generators for hospitals. Parallel redundancy multiplies reliability — if each component works 90 percent of the time, two in parallel work 99 percent — but only when failures are independent; a single flood can drown both pumps. Engineers distinguish active redundancy (all units running) from standby (spares waiting), and they test failover, because redundancy that has never been tested is hope. The demo computes parallel reliability.
capabilities: Spares so failure is not catastrophe
Parallel math: two 90% units make 99%
Independent failures required: one flood drowns both pumps
Active vs standby redundancy, and tested failover

title: The Concepts Database — Optimization
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Optimization finds the best choice within constraints: the cheapest route, the strongest shape for its weight, the schedule that finishes first. Every optimization names an objective (what is best), variables (what can change), and constraints (what is allowed). Methods range from calculus on smooth problems to grid search, hill climbing, and evolutionary algorithms on rough ones. The honest caveat: optimizers find the best answer to the stated problem, and a wrongly stated problem gets a perfectly wrong answer. The demo grid-searches a parabola's minimum.
capabilities: Objective, variables, and constraints named first
Methods: calculus, grid search, hill climbing, evolutionary
Optimizers answer the stated problem — state it right
Trade-offs: the Pareto frontier of competing goals

title: The Concepts Database — Signal versus noise
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Signal is the message; noise is everything else. The signal-to-noise ratio measures how far the message stands above the clutter — in decibels, where every 10 dB is a tenfold power ratio. Engineers raise SNR by amplifying carefully, filtering ruthlessly, averaging repeated measurements, and shielding against interference. The deeper lesson generalizes: in data, in news, in arguments, the skill is the same — find the signal, name the noise, and do not mistake loud noise for strong signal. The demo computes SNR and shows averaging beating down noise.
capabilities: Signal as message, noise as everything else
SNR in decibels: 10 dB per tenfold power
Raising SNR: amplify, filter, average, shield
The general skill: find signal, name noise
